findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access mask (0x1F3FFF) by attacker PowerShell on scranton and via WinRM on nashua
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z, and again with 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z. The matching Security 4656 event (record 73759) shows the same process requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe, explicitly including 'Read from process memory' and 'Write to process memory' — the access pattern of an LSASS memory dump. This occurred inside a pbeesly PowerShell session that also ran attacker tooling (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-ScreenCapture, accesschk.exe). On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM remote PowerShell, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.430Z, the same full-access LSASS read via remote PowerShell. The remaining LSASS opens (svchost.exe 0x1000, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400, wininit/csrss at process start) are normal system behaviour.

findings.title: SAM registry access and HKLM\SECURITY\Cache writes are all by lsass.exe (SYSTEM) — benign
findings.summary: Security 4656 events show SAM_SERVER (Object Name 'SAM'), SAM_DOMAIN ('SCRANTON') and SAM_ALIAS handle requests on scranton.dmevals.local, but every one is issued by lsass.exe itself under account SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, Logon ID 0x3E7) — normal LSA operation, not an external dumping tool. Likewise the Sysmon event.code 13 registry writes to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua (PID 728) and scranton (PID 748) are performed by lsass.exe, the legitimate owner of the SECURITY hive cache. No reg save / hive-copy of SAM or SECURITY was observed (C019/C020/C024 zero hits).

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local (benign)
findings.summary: On 2020-05-01 23:19 (2020-05-02T03:19Z) on scranton.dmevals.local, the legitimate Azure NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (running as SYSTEM, parent services.exe) launched netsh.exe with 'trace start capture=yes' writing an .etl capture file to C:\windows\TEMP, then 'netsh trace stop' ~7s later. This is the standard Azure Network Watcher packet-capture feature, not adversary sniffing. No sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap), no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads, and no promiscuous-mode or raw-socket indicators were found in any dataset.

findings.title: No network sniffing tooling or capture drivers observed

findings.title: LSASS credential access observed (T1003-like), not MFA interception
findings.summary: Although not MFA interception, the closest credential-access activity is LSASS process access. On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access) and 0x1f3fff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29. These high-access LSASS reads are consistent with credential dumping (T1003), not T1111. The remaining 300+ lsass accesses are low-access (0x1000/0x1400) from svchost.exe and security products and are benign.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:22, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on port 445 and was rejected (conn_state REJ, history 'Sr', 5 attempts 00:32:14.891-00:32:17.069). It then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80 using the Windows WebDAV redirector (user_agent 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362'), issuing OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/HEAD/UNLOCK against http://192.168.0.4/webdav/ and successfully creating /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z (PUT -> 201 Created). The PUT request carried an AUTHORIZATION header, i.e. the victim host transmitted credentials to the attacker-controlled server. This is the classic T1187 forced-authentication pattern: a UNC/WebDAV path (\\192.168.0.4\webdav\OfficeSupplies.7z) coerces the victim into authenticating to an attacker listener, leaking NTLM material. The activity is preceded by PowerShell Gallery / oneget CDN access (www.powershellgallery.com, onegetcdn.azureedge.net, go.microsoft.com at 00:31-00:32), consistent with a package-install or scripted workflow used to trigger the coercion. All 36 WebDAV requests originate solely from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: Checks for browser credential artifacts (Login Data, logins.json, cookies) in Sysmon process/file events, Security object access, PowerShell script blocks and other channels returned no hits. The only file event matching a cookie path was a benign system file (INetCookies under the LocalService WARP JIT package profile) on scranton, not a browser credential store. No evidence of web-browser credential theft in the available windows.sysmon/security/powershell/other data.

findings.title: LSASS handle access consistent with Credential Manager/DPAPI harvesting; no vaultcmd/cmdkey usage
findings.summary: The full-access LSASS handles opened by pbeesly's PowerShell (scranton, 0x1FFFFF) and wsmprovhost (nashua, 0x1F3FFF) are the mechanism by which Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI secrets held in LSASS memory are harvested. No explicit vaultcmd/cmdkey command lines or Credentials-file writes were observed (those checks returned zero hits), and the only 'Credential' text in windows.other was a benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' event on scranton. The LSASS access itself is the malicious indicator.

findings.title: Benign LSASS access by system processes and Azure guest tooling
findings.summary: Most LSASS handle events are routine: wininit.exe/csrss.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF at scranton 03:19:09 (process startup), svchost.exe with 0x101001, CollectGuestLogs.exe (C:\WindowsAzure\Packages) with 0x1410/0x10 on scranton/utica/newyork/nashua, and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe with 0x1FFFFF on scranton. The sdelete64.exe LSASS event on nashua is LSASS (SourceImage lsass.exe) accessing sdelete64.exe via lsasrv.dll/SspiSrv.dll/RPCRT4.dll — normal SSPI/RPC, not sdelete reading LSASS. These are expected system behaviours, not credential theft.

On 2020-05-02 03:05:16 UTC, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS / full read-write), the classic signature of an in-memory credential dump. This is the same host where user pbeesly ran a malicious PowerShell chain minutes later (03:21:27-03:21:29): a registry-stored payload read from HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft 'value Supplement' piped to Invoke-Expression, an obfuscated P/Invoke helper resolving GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle, and a Gzip+Base64 hidden PowerShell launcher. The LSASS handle access is the credential-theft step of this intrusion; it is not a modification of the authentication process itself (no password filter, reversible encryption, MFA, hybrid identity or network provider DLL changes were observed).

findings.summary: The 218 LogonType 3 (network) 4624 events are dominated by machine-account Kerberos logons: NEWYORK$ (from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429, 10.0.0.4), SCRANTON$ (10.0.1.4), NASHUA$ (10.0.1.6), UTICA$ (10.0.1.5) and WEC$ (10.0.1.10), all with LogonProcessName 'Kerberos'. These are routine computer-account authentications between domain members and the DC, not evidence of a DC authentication backdoor. The only non-machine account is pbeesly (13 logons from 10.0.1.4, 5 with no source, 1 from 10.0.1.6, 1 NtLmSsp from 172.18.39.2), consistent with the compromised user's lateral movement rather than a modified DC authentication process. findings.title: Machine-account Kerberos network logons (normal DC authentication, no backdoor)

findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioned in the middle. The only network-level oddity is in the zeek capture (2020-04-30 window): responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answers for many unrelated destination IPs (192.168.0.4, 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, 192.168.0.5) and source 10.0.1.4 appears with two MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1). 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic/placeholder MAC, so this is a capture artifact rather than a real host impersonating others. SMB/RPC traffic is normal domain activity (SAMR/LSAR to the DC, IPC$ mapping).

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; service installs are built-in/PSEXESVC
findings.summary: Sysmon DNS queries (event 22) show only normal lookups (host FQDNs, LDAP SRV records, Microsoft telemetry, wpad) with no LLMNR/NBT-NS-style poisoning, and no Responder/MITM/LLMNR/NBT-NS strings appear in PowerShell script blocks. The 23 event.code 4697 service installations are Windows built-in per-user services (svchost UnistackSvcGroup etc.) plus PSEXESVC (%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, installed by user pbeesly on nashua) and javamtsup (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe on scranton) — these are lateral-movement/execution artifacts, not SMB relay. findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; duplicate MAC-to-IP mappings are capture artifacts
findings.summary: Stacking source and responder MACs in the zeek conn log shows no host claiming multiple IPs in a way consistent with ARP spoofing. Source 10.0.1.4 appears with two MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and the responder 12:34:56:78:9a:bc (a synthetic placeholder MAC) answers for several distinct IPs — both are artifacts of the capture rather than gratuitous ARP. findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP telemetry present in any dataset
findings.summary: No DHCP-related activity is observable. The zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/weird/smb_mapping/notice/pe). windows.other contains no DHCP event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063). findings.title: LSASS memory access with full access mask by PowerShell on scranton — Kerberos ticket theft precursor
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a fileless credential-theft chain: hostui.bat -> hostui.exe (runas) -> powershell.exe -c "Get-ItemPropertyValue 'HKLM:\\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' | Invoke-Expression", which decoded a base64/gzip loader and a reflective shellcode loader (GetProcAddress/ReflectedDelegate). The PowerShell process then opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), the access mask used to read Kerberos TGT/TGS tickets and other secrets from LSASS memory. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM) also opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF. These are the credential-access actions that precede Kerberos ticket theft.

findings.title: Anomalous krbtgt service-ticket requests from SCRANTON$ on newyork
findings.summary: On newyork.dmevals.local, the machine account SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL requested Kerberos service tickets for the krbtgt service (Service ID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-502) with TicketOptions 0x60810010, alongside repeated TGS requests for NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$. Requests for a krbtgt service ticket are unusual and are consistent with forged/abused ticket activity (golden-ticket style). All 28 4769 events used encryption type 0x12 (AES256), so no RC4 downgrade was observed.

findings.title: No silver-ticket evidence observed
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local were all issued by the KDC with encryption type 0x12 (AES256) and normal TicketOptions; no service tickets were observed being used without a corresponding KDC-issued request, and no forged service-ticket artifacts (e.g. anomalous SPN usage) were found. findings.title: No Kerberoasting pattern observed
findings.summary: Zeek Kerberos records (2020-04-30 window, non-overlapping with the Windows data) show only normal pbeesly AS/TGS traffic to krbtgt, cifs/NASHUA, host/nashua.dmevals.local, HTTP/NASHUA and ldap/NEWYORK, with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED on AS requests. findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting evidence observed
findings.summary: Zeek Kerberos AS requests all returned KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (pre-authentication required) before succeeding, indicating accounts are not configured with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication'. No AS-REP roasting tooling strings (AS-REP, GetNPUsers, DontRequirePreAuth) were found in PowerShell script blocks.
